name: Opus 5 dispersion
strategy: Equal-weight 51% long basket of twelve large caps screened for the highest idiosyncratic (residual-to-SPY) volatility and the lowest mutual correlation across eight sectors, hedged with a 47% short of the cap-weighted indices they sit in (28% SPY + 19% QQQ, the split that minimised residual volatility across five half-year windows), leaving 2% cash and roughly zero net index beta.

positions.thesis: Managed care and still the purest single-name scatter in the screen: ~52% vol, ~99% idiosyncratic, measured beta 0.35, driven by MA rate notices, star ratings and utilisation trend with no index analogue. Q2 adjusted EPS $7.61 on revenue +26%, and the sell side has been converging my way since late July (Morgan Stanley to Equal Weight 4 Aug, Piper to Overweight 30 July, Barclays PT $407). The 2027 exit from plans covering ~600k members and the recovery from the 3.61 average 2026 star rating toward the 3% pretax margin target run on a dated, company-specific clock that the index cannot price.

Consumer finance, and the highest-idiosyncratic-volatility large cap in its sector. The volatility is calendar-driven rather than macro: Discover card migration flipping through the second half of 2026, back book by Q1 2027, $2.5bn of synergies by 2027. Q2 adjusted EPS $5.81 against $4.85 consensus with credit costs down sharply sequentially. The July retail-sales miss is the live bear case on the credit side, which is exactly the two-sidedness the mandate wants, and integration milestones have no index analogue.

Discount retail: ~46% vol, ~96% idiosyncratic, driven by comp-store prints and banner restructuring, with a trade-down profile that runs against the cyclicals elsewhere in the basket rather than with them. The Section 301 forced-labour tariffs were finalised 23 July so the import-cost shock was in the price before I entered. The Q2 print is now dated to 27 August against a guide of $4.8-4.9bn sales, comps +2.5-3.5% and adjusted EPS $1.00-1.15, and a consumer trading down after a 0.6% retail-sales decline is a tailwind here where it is a headwind for the discretionary legs.

Nitrogen fertiliser: the return function is the natural gas feedstock spread and crop economics, with essentially no equity-index loading. The 5 August print lifted the mid-cycle EBITDA target to $2.9bn, guided nitrogen tightness through 2030, raised the dividend 20% and showed gas cost down 11% y/y. It gave back 2.6% this week as the weakest leg in the basket, which is precisely the point of holding it: with a single AI factor still dominating cross-asset correlation, a name that trades on gas and grain is the cleanest correlation diversifier available.

Cruise: ~54% vol with a large booking-curve-driven company-specific component sitting on top of a cyclical beta the index short already absorbs. Q2 adjusted EPS $4.21 vs $3.98, FY guide raised to $17.73-17.87, record booking activity and accelerated buybacks, against fuel, airfare and softness in Mediterranean and West-Mexico itineraries. With sentiment at 51 the consumer bear case has real teeth here, which is the two-sided idiosyncratic debate I want; tighter 18% stop because it carries the highest beta in the basket.

The one semiconductor long I keep, because its ~63% vol is 76% idiosyncratic and driven by licensing and customer concentration rather than the AI capex cycle. Fiscal Q3 beat on revenue and posted the first EPS miss in seven quarters, and Apple modem revenue is guided to fall faster than previously flagged from fiscal Q4 as Apple's in-house share rises. I hold it because customer concentration resolving on its own clock is the residual, offset by the 1 September price increases, initial hyperscaler datacentre shipments due December 2026 and the $5bn FY27 / $15bn FY29 targets. Sized at the basket weight, not on conviction.

Energy, the basket's macro-offset leg: crude-driven returns are the classic low-correlation block and measured beta is near zero. The 5 August print was a blowout — adjusted EPS $2.40 vs $1.87 on revenue $8.33bn vs $7.18bn, realised crude $96.78, production above the top of guidance, Midstream pre-tax $961m above guide and $1.9bn of debt retired in one quarter against the $10bn target. Held for orthogonality to the other eleven rather than for a crude view, with the deleveraging clock as a company-specific catalyst in its own right.

Biotech: ~72% vol, ~90% idiosyncratic, pipeline binaries being the archetypal dispersion asset, and the best leg in the basket this week at +5.9%. mFluvis is approved for adults 50+ as the first US mRNA influenza vaccine, mCOMBRIAX cleared in Europe, and mRNA-1469 has entered Phase 1 for Ebola — three separate platform-specific events in ten days with no index content whatsoever. Still 31% below the $85.60 July high, so the two-sided debate between the 2026-27 flu launch and cash guided to $4.7-5.2bn at year end is genuinely live. No take-profit: the binary I bought it for has resolved and it is now an ordinary scatter asset. Wide 22% stop because burn is the bear case.

Aerospace. 777X certification is arguably the largest purely company-specific binary in US large cap — over 55% of certification flight testing complete, a fifth test aircraft added, first delivery promised for 2027 and already slipped once, with no index analogue and zero AI-factor loading. The operating base is turning: record $715bn backlog, 171 Q2 deliveries and +$631m free cash flow after four quarters of burn. The debate stayed usefully two-sided this week with Argus double-upgrading to Buy on 11 August against RBC's more conservative certification assumptions, and the Archer stake adds an option with its own clock.

Cable and communications, the highest residual volatility available at this market cap and none of it with any index or AI-factor content — the stock has halved over a year inside a $111.55-$285.82 range. The debate is entirely company-specific and got sharper this week: broadband erosion at 172k lost subs in Q2 against 406k mobile line adds to 12.5m, and the CPUC cleared the $34.5bn Cox merger on 13 August, removing the last regulatory barrier to a deal that adds ~6m customers. The concurrent shelf filing and 2038/2041 secured-note exchange put balance-sheet execution on the clock too. Wide 22% stop because the tape here is violent in both directions.

Autos, and the leg I most want for correlation reasons. The return function is tariffs, pricing and input costs rather than anything the index trades on: $2.5-3.5bn of gross tariff cost and $1.5-2bn of commodity and DRAM cost against a $500m refund after the Supreme Court struck the IEEPA tariffs, with adjusted EPS guidance raised to $12-14. The DRAM line is the point — GM's cost base is directly hurt by the same memory squeeze lifting the AI complex, making this one of the few large caps with a negative loading on the factor currently dominating cross-asset correlation. July retail sales showed the weakness concentrated in autos, which is the bear case doing its job on a name I hold for scatter, not direction.

New, replacing PYPL: gold mining, measured beta ~0.4 and near-zero correlation to any of the other eleven legs — the best score in the whole screen on the mandate's second criterion, which is what I need after this week left five of twelve legs levered to the same consumer. It is also the only large cap here that is structurally long the specific state of the world that would hurt the rest of the basket: gold at $4,373/oz with futures pricing a 30.6% chance of a September hike and zero chance of a cut. Deliberately two-sided at entry — record $2.2bn Q2 free cash flow, $1.9bn returned, 100m+ shares bought back and FY26 reaffirmed at ~$8.5bn FCF, against attributable production falling to ~5.3moz on the Nevada Gold Mines and Pueblo Viejo transitions, AISC rising to ~$1,680/oz, a slight revenue and EPS miss, and a stock already +24% in a month into Friday's profit-taking. Ordinary 20% stop.

Primary hedge, restored to the mandate's stated size. A long book that is managed care, consumer finance, discount retail, nitrogen, cruise, mobile semis, energy, biotech, aerospace, cable, autos and gold carries broad-market beta rather than Nasdaq beta, so the broad index is the residual-vol-minimising instrument against it. At 28% SPY plus 19% QQQ the hedge is worth ~0.50 of beta against ~0.49 from the 51% basket on fundamental betas — net index beta straddling zero, which is the mandate's operative constraint and the thing my 44% version last week failed. No take-profit: a hedge that closes itself into a 7% index drawdown would leave the book 51% net long at the exact moment it is doing its job.

Secondary hedge, returned to the mandate's 28:19 split from the 28:16 I ran for a week. That split was calibrated to minimise residual volatility across five half-year windows; my reduction to 16% was calibrated to one week of observed basket beta, which is not enough evidence to override it, and it is exactly the kind of tape-driven re-cutting that cost me on 30 July when I ran 21% as a bet on mega-cap concentration unwinding. QQQ outran SPY again this week (+1.42% vs +0.43%), which is a reason to carry the mandated Nasdaq hedge rather than a reason to guess at it. Take-profit removed for the same reason as SPY: the hedge must survive the drawdown it exists to absorb.

reassessment_note: Weekly desk 2026-08-15: Two things, one forced and one overdue. (1) PYPL stopped being a dispersion asset this week. WSJ reported Friday that Stripe/Advent talks are advancing toward a deal in coming weeks, and the stock closed $61.66 against a standing $60.50 bid the board already rejected. I now own a merger spread at a negative basis, not a debate about branded checkout: the payoff is roughly -2% if a deal signs near the bid, about +5% on a bump, and -20% to -25% back toward the $47.37 pre-bid price if talks break, in a gap my -20% stop would be jumped straight through. My screen selects for high residual volatility that is two-sided; a signed deal collapses that volatility into an antitrust-timing spread with capped upside. Being paid +4.4% since entry and ~30% above the pre-bid price to exit an asymmetry I was never mandated to hold is the easy half of this decision. (2) I am putting the hedge back to the mandate's own arithmetic — 51% long, 28% SPY + 19% QQQ. Last week I ran 54/44 on the argument that the basket's realised beta is far below one and 47% over-hedges it. That argument rested on a single week's observation, against a 28/19 split calibrated to minimise residual volatility across five half-year windows, and it left a +10-point net-long notional tilt and roughly +0.10 of net index beta that my mandate does not authorise. On fundamental betas the basket at 51% carries ~0.49 against a 47% hedge worth ~0.50 — net beta essentially zero, which is the operative constraint. The turnover to get there is about 15% of NAV at ~2bps, so cost is not a reason to keep an unauthorised tilt. Replacing PYPL with NEM also fixes a correlation problem the week exposed: July retail sales fell 0.6% and sentiment dropped to 51, and five of my twelve legs were consumer-spending assets that would move as one in a consumer-led downturn. A gold miner with ~0.4 beta and near-zero correlation to the other eleven is the correction the screen would make itself.
novelty: This book is the only one I run — it is a single equal-weighted twelve-name residual-volatility basket carried fully index-hedged to zero net beta, and it shares no leg, no sizing rule and no directional expression with any other book, since every position is held for its idiosyncratic clock rather than for a view on where the market goes.
research_notes:
WEEK RECONSTRUCTION (Aug 10 close -> Aug 14 close, my entry basis). Indices: SPY 773.03 -> 776.34 (+0.43%); QQQ 720.87 -> 731.07 (+1.42%). S&P set a record above 7,800 Thursday then gave 0.2% back Friday on weak data; third straight weekly gain, Russell 2000 at a record.

MY TWELVE LONGS, priced individually: PYPL 59.07->61.66 (+4.4%), MRNA 59.81->63.32 (+5.9%), COF 218.97->227.34 (+3.8%), QCOM 162.17->165.79 (+2.2%), HUM 385.70->389.05 (+0.9%), CHTR 153.29->154.27 (+0.6%), DLTR 129.37->129.39 (0.0%), OXY 58.65->58.36 (-0.5%), BA 232.79->231.67 (-0.5%), RCL 308.00->305.00 (-1.0%), GM 87.96->86.77 (-1.4%), CF 121.48->118.30 (-2.6%). Equal-weight basket +0.99% vs SPY +0.43%. Attribution: longs 0.54 x 0.99 = +0.53%, hedge -(0.28x0.43 + 0.16x1.42) = -0.35%, net roughly +0.18% for the week; the round is still -0.52% cumulative, drawdown -1.96%. The structure did what it is supposed to do — basket beat the index, hedge cost what it should, dispersion inside the basket was wide (+5.9% to -2.6% in four sessions) and driven by name-specific news, not one factor.

THE MATERIAL EVENT — PYPL. WSJ reported Aug 14 that Stripe and Advent talks to buy PayPal are advancing and a deal could come together "in coming weeks"; TechCrunch and CNBC corroborated. The standing offer is $60.50/share (~$53bn), first made 15 July, which the PayPal board rejected as undervaluing the company. Pre-bid close was $47.37 (14 July). PYPL now trades $61.66 — ABOVE the standing bid. That inverts the leg's return function: I am no longer holding a two-sided debate about branded-checkout share and take rate, I am holding a merger-arb position at a negative spread. Payoff on a deal struck near the current bid is roughly -2%; on a modest bump to $65, +5%; on talks collapsing, the reference point is $47.37, i.e. -20% to -25% in a gap that my -20% stop would be jumped through. Residual volatility also collapses once a deal is signed — the stock becomes a spread on antitrust timing (Stripe+PayPal in online payments faces serious US and EU scrutiny), which is the opposite of the high-residual-vol, two-sided asset my screen selects for.

OTHER NAMES CHECKED. CHTR: CPUC approved the $34.5bn Cox merger 13 Aug, the last regulatory barrier; combined ~37m subs. The company also filed a shelf and launched an exchange offer on the 2038/2041 secured notes. Deal-closing mechanics now sit on top of the broadband-loss debate — still entirely company-specific, no index content. Thesis intact. MRNA: mFluvis approved for 50+, mCOMBRIAX combo approved in Europe, Ebola candidate mRNA-1469 into Phase 1; stock +5.9% on the week but still -31% over a month from the $85.60 July high. Pipeline binaries continue to fire on their own clock. QCOM: recovered 2.2% after the fiscal-Q3 print (revenue beat, first EPS miss in seven quarters); hyperscaler datacentre initial shipments still guided to December 2026; dividend $0.92 ex-3 Sep. DLTR: Q2 print confirmed for 27 Aug (guide $4.8-4.9bn sales, comps +2.5-3.5%, adj EPS $1.00-1.15) — the dated catalyst I own it for is now inside the window. BA: Argus double-upgrade to Buy 11 Aug, Archer Aviation deal giving Boeing a 19.75% stake and board seat, $132m of contracts; 777X still the 2027 binary. COF: Discover card migration flipping through H2, integration on schedule, FY26 EPS ~$20.19. HUM, OXY, CF, GM, RCL: no thesis-changing news.

MACRO. This is the part that changes my correlation thinking. July retail sales -0.6%, the first decline in nine months and the largest in 14, with weakness concentrated in autos and non-store; UMich preliminary August sentiment 51, down ~8%. Fed funds futures price a 69.4% chance of a HOLD at 3.50-3.75% on 15-16 September with 30.6% on a HIKE — no cut priced at all. Gold $4,373/oz Friday after a two-month high, up ~$1,019 y/y. The consumer is the single visible common factor in my basket right now: COF, RCL, GM, DLTR and PYPL are five of twelve legs that would move together in a consumer-led downturn. That is a mutual-correlation problem the screen exists to prevent.

REPLACEMENT CANDIDATE. Newmont (NEM, $117.76): gold miner, measured beta ~0.4, near-zero correlation to any of the other eleven, and the only large-cap return stream that is structurally long the exact scenario (sticky inflation with a hiking Fed and a softening consumer) that would hurt the rest of my basket. Q2 on 23 July: record $2.2bn free cash flow, $2.9bn operating cash flow, adj EPS $2.10 on $6.12bn (both slightly short of consensus), $1.8-1.9bn returned, 100m+ shares repurchased cumulatively, FY26 guidance reaffirmed at ~5.3moz attributable and ~$8.5bn FCF. The bear case is live and company-specific: production declining y/y on the Nevada Gold Mines and Pueblo Viejo transitions, AISC rising to ~$1,680/oz on royalties and lower by-product credits, and the stock is +24% in a month so it is extended. Consensus PT ~$131. I considered FCX instead and rejected it — copper carries growth beta, which defeats the point.
